q: The Doppler effect or Doppler shift is the change in frequency of a wave related to an observer due to the relative motion between the source and observer.
e: True. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it.

q: Usually, only the motion of the source and the observer directly towards or away from each other in the reference frame in which the wave medium is considered at rest.
e: True. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed.

q: A common example of Doppler shift is the change of frequency (pitch) heard when a vehicle sounding a horn approach and recedes from an observer.
e: True. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other.

q: A common example of Doppler shift is the change of amplitude heard when a vehicle sounding a horn approach and recedes from an observer.
e: False. The everyday Doppler example is a change of frequency, heard as pitch, as a horn approaches and recedes. Amplitude is loudness, not that sliding note. Approach raises pitch; recession lowers it.

q: There are three cases we encounter in Doppler effect.
e: True. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Three cases we encounter in Doppler effect cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: $f_o$ is frequency heard by the observer.
e: True. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed.

q: $f_s$ is frequency produced by the source.
e: True. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it.

q: $v$ is speed of sound in the medium.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. V is speed of sound in the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: $+v_o$ is used when the observer moves towards the source.
e: True. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it.

q: $+v_o$ is used when the observer moves away from the source.
e: False. Plus v_o is for an observer moving toward the source, which raises the observed frequency. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. The source signs are chosen the same way: approach up, recession down.

q: $-v_o$ is used when the observer moves away from the source.
e: True. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency. Away from the source you flip that observer sign. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium.

q: $-v_s$ is used when the source moves towards the observer.
e: True. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency.

q: $+v_s$ is used when the source moves away from the observer.
e: True. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. Plus vo is toward the source, which raises frequency.

q: When observer and source are stationary, $v_o = v_s = 0$.
e: True. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium. In Doppler formulas, fo is what the observer hears and vo is the observer's speed. Away from the source you flip that observer sign.

q: The wavelength of light from a star observed from the earth shifts towards the red end of the spectrum when the earth and the star are moving away from each other.
e: True. Monochromatic work uses one lambda so patterns do not smear. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet.

q: The phenomenon of light shifting towards the red end of the spectrum is called blue shift.
e: False. Motion apart slides light to the red, longer wavelength, and that is red shift. Blue shift is approach, toward shorter wavelength. Stars receding from Earth are the red-shift case.

q: The velocity of the astronomical body moving away from the earth can be determined from the fractional change in wavelength.
e: True. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet. Monochromatic work uses one lambda so patterns do not smear. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating.

q: If the star were approaching the earth the spectral lines would shift towards blue end.
e: True. star and approaching have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of star would describe a different law.

q: Radar (radio detection and ranging) is a form of echolocation that uses electromagnetic waves instead of sound.
e: True. Bats navigate and hunt that way. Sonar is the engineered version in water. Radar is radio detection and ranging: electromagnetic echolocation.

q: Radar (radio detection and ranging) is a form of echolocation that uses sound waves instead of electromagnetic waves.
e: False. Radar uses electromagnetic waves, not sound. Sonar is the sound version. The ranging idea is similar; the wave family is not.

q: The Doppler effect is used in some types of radar, to measure the velocity of detected objects.
e: True. A bat's hunt is sound, not radar. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it.

q: Doppler ultrasound is a technique that is used to examine blood flow.
e: True. Infrasound is the low-frequency counterpart. Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other. Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it.

q: Blood flow rates can be found by measuring Doppler shift in frequency of ultrasound reflected by red blood cell (known as angiodynography).
e: True. Amplitude, loudness, is not that sliding pitch. Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, too high for the human ear. Short wavelength gives sharp echoes for imaging and ranging.
